journal.book:
MY PLAYBOOK

Why I am doing this
- Being fully present with the people I love
- Clear mornings and steady energy
- Becoming someone I am proud of

My rule
I log slips instead of hiding them. A slip is data, not a reset.

If this, then that
If I am in bed late at night, then Get up and leave the room for 10 minutes. Water, stretch, tidy something. Then back to bed without my phone.
If I am lonely or low, then Text or call one person. A message counts. Or go somewhere with people around.
If I am bored or idle, then 10-minute walk outside, or 10 minutes on a hobby or project.
If I am stressed or anxious, then Move my body (walk, pushups), then write one sentence about what is stressing me.

If I slip
1. Log it in 30 seconds. No hiding.
2. One small action within the hour: water, step outside, or text someone.
3. No big decisions tonight, and no "I blew it" verdicts.
4. Tomorrow: check in as usual. Nothing resets. Ask what the trigger was and what to change.
5. If I want to, tell my safe person: "I slipped."

What I have learned
1. You do not need to feel ready: No. Mixed feelings are a normal part of change. Start with one small step, and let your own reasons carry it.
2. Urges are waves: An urge rises, peaks, and passes. You do not have to fight it or obey it. Notice it, breathe, and outlast this one.
5. Name the act, not yourself: Describe what you did, not who you are: “I slipped last night,” not “I am a failure.” Then protect your next good move.
8. Wanting to be loved: No. A habit is something you do, not a verdict on whether you can love. Honesty and closeness are skills you can start practicing now.
11. What to call it, and who can help: No. You can use your own words. What counts is what it does to your life, and help is there whatever you call it.
12. What getting better looks like: Getting better is growth with setbacks, across a whole life: health, home, purpose, and people. A streak is one part, not the whole picture.
13. Name the feeling: Urges often ride in on a feeling. Name it in a word or two, and it loses some of its grip. Then meet that feeling another way.
15. Move your body: Yes. A short burst of movement eases cravings for a while. When an urge starts, move first, then decide.
17. The first link in the chain: Usually hours earlier, with small choices that look harmless. Catch an early link, while the urge is quiet, and the last one never forms.
20. Fewer fights, not more willpower: Not mostly. People with strong self-control fight temptation less, not more. Arrange your day so the fight happens less, and count the fights you skip.
21. Missing a day: No. A single missed day barely dents a new habit, but misses add up. The day after, come back in the smallest way.
22. When values and habits clash: Ask what bothers you most: losing control, a clash with your values, or both. Each points to different help, and both are real.
23. Plan the empty hour: Do not wait to feel like it. Put a real, small activity in your hardest hour, and do it even if you do not feel like it.
24. What therapy is like: Yes, treatment appears to help, and one kind, CBT, has the strongest support. Ask how a therapist works, and switch if it does not fit.
26. SMART Recovery: four points and a toolbox: Yes. SMART Recovery teaches practical tools for motivation, urges, thoughts and feelings, and a balanced life. You can borrow them with or without a meeting.
28. Why groups help: Groups change who you spend time with, and that is one of the main ways they help. Start small: listen at one meeting, or ask one person to check in.
31. Guilt, shame, and God: Write it honestly, then tell God and one safe person. Guilt can point you toward change. Shame says to hide.

MY PLAYBOOK

Why I am doing this
- Being fully present with the people I love
- Clear mornings and steady energy
- Becoming someone I am proud of

My rule
I log slips instead of hiding them. A slip is data, not a reset.

If this, then that
If I am in bed late at night, then Get up and leave the room for 10 minutes. Water, stretch, tidy something. Then back to bed without my phone.
If I am lonely or low, then Text or call one person. A message counts. Or go somewhere with people around.
If I am bored or idle, then 10-minute walk outside, or 10 minutes on a hobby or project.
If I am stressed or anxious, then Move my body (walk, pushups), then write one sentence about what is stressing me.

If I slip
1. Log it in 30 seconds. No hiding.
2. One small action within the hour: water, step outside, or text someone.
3. No big decisions tonight, and no "I blew it" verdicts.
4. Tomorrow: check in as usual. Nothing resets. Ask what the trigger was and what to change.
5. If I want to, tell my safe person: "I slipped."

What I have learned
1. You do not need to feel ready: No. Mixed feelings are a normal part of change. Start with one small step, and let your own reasons carry it.
2. Urges are waves: An urge rises, peaks, and passes. You do not have to fight it or obey it. Notice it, breathe, and outlast this one.
5. Name the act, not yourself: Describe what you did, not who you are: “I slipped last night,” not “I am a failure.” Then protect your next good move.
8. Wanting to be loved: No. A habit is something you do, not a verdict on whether you can love. Honesty and closeness are skills you can start practicing now.
11. What to call it, and who can help: No. You can use your own words. What counts is what it does to your life, and help is there whatever you call it.
12. What getting better looks like: Getting better is growth with setbacks, across a whole life: health, home, purpose, and people. A streak is one part, not the whole picture.
13. Name the feeling: Urges often ride in on a feeling. Name it in a word or two, and it loses some of its grip. Then meet that feeling another way.
15. Move your body: Yes. A short burst of movement eases cravings for a while. When an urge starts, move first, then decide.
17. The first link in the chain: Usually hours earlier, with small choices that look harmless. Catch an early link, while the urge is quiet, and the last one never forms.
20. Fewer fights, not more willpower: Not mostly. People with strong self-control fight temptation less, not more. Arrange your day so the fight happens less, and count the fights you skip.
21. Missing a day: No. A single missed day barely dents a new habit, but misses add up. The day after, come back in the smallest way.
22. When values and habits clash: Ask what bothers you most: losing control, a clash with your values, or both. Each points to different help, and both are real.
23. Plan the empty hour: Do not wait to feel like it. Put a real, small activity in your hardest hour, and do it even if you do not feel like it.
24. What therapy is like: Yes, treatment appears to help, and one kind, CBT, has the strongest support. Ask how a therapist works, and switch if it does not fit.
26. SMART Recovery: four points and a toolbox: Yes. SMART Recovery teaches practical tools for motivation, urges, thoughts and feelings, and a balanced life. You can borrow them with or without a meeting.
28. Why groups help: Groups change who you spend time with, and that is one of the main ways they help. Start small: listen at one meeting, or ask one person to check in.
31. Guilt, shame, and God: Write it honestly, then tell God and one safe person. Guilt can point you toward change. Shame says to hide.

5Name the act, not yourselfFinished Sep 7, read again once (last Sep 22)DoneThe one thing to keepDescribe what you did, not who you are: “I slipped last night,” not “I am a failure.” Then protect your next good move.
6Kindness after a slipBeing kind to yourself helped people do better, not worse.1–5 min
6Kindness after a slipBeing kind to yourself helped people do better, not worse.1–5 min
7Secrets are heavyCarrying it alone costs more than it seems.1–5 min
7Secrets are heavyCarrying it alone costs more than it seems.1–5 min
8Wanting to be lovedA habit is not a verdict on whether you can love.Done
8Wanting to be lovedFinished Aug 20DoneThe one thing to keepNo. A habit is something you do, not a verdict on whether you can love. Honesty and closeness are skills you can start practicing now.
9If this, then thatDecide now, so you do not have to decide at 1 AM.1–5 min
9If this, then thatDecide now, so you do not have to decide at 1 AM.1–5 min
10Change the settingHabits live in places. Move the cue.1–5 min

12What getting better looks likeNot a straight line. Not perfect. Real.Done

12What getting better looks likeFinished Jul 18, read again on 2 days (last Sep 18)DoneThe one thing to keepGetting better is growth with setbacks, across a whole life: health, home, purpose, and people. A streak is one part, not the whole picture.
13Name the feelingPutting a word on it can turn the volume down.Done
13Name the feelingFinished Aug 19DoneThe one thing to keepUrges often ride in on a feeling. Name it in a word or two, and it loses some of its grip. Then meet that feeling another way.

15Move your bodyA short burst of movement eases cravings.Done
15Move your bodyFinished Sep 30DoneThe one thing to keepYes. A short burst of movement eases cravings for a while. When an urge starts, move first, then decide.
16Thoughts are not ordersYou can have the thought and still choose.1–5 min
16Thoughts are not ordersYou can have the thought and still choose.1–5 min
17The first link in the chainA slip often starts hours earlier, with a small yes.Done

17The first link in the chainFinished Sep 22DoneThe one thing to keepUsually hours earlier, with small choices that look harmless. Catch an early link, while the urge is quiet, and the last one never forms.

21Missing a dayFinished Oct 7, read again onceDoneThe one thing to keepNo. A single missed day barely dents a new habit, but misses add up. The day after, come back in the smallest way.

23Plan the empty hourWaiting to feel like it does not work. Put it on the calendar.Done

journal.book:
MY PLAYBOOK

Why I am doing this
- Being fully present with the people I love
- Clear mornings and steady energy
- Becoming someone I am proud of

My rule
I log slips instead of hiding them. A slip is data, not a reset.

If this, then that
If I am in bed late at night, then Get up and leave the room for 10 minutes. Water, stretch, tidy something. Then back to bed without my phone.
If I am lonely or low, then Text or call one person. A message counts. Or go somewhere with people around.
If I am bored or idle, then 10-minute walk outside, or 10 minutes on a hobby or project.
If I am stressed or anxious, then Move my body (walk, pushups), then write one sentence about what is stressing me.

If I slip
1. Log it in 30 seconds. No hiding.
2. One small action within the hour: water, step outside, or text someone.
3. No big decisions tonight, and no "I blew it" verdicts.
4. Tomorrow: check in as usual. Nothing resets. Ask what the trigger was and what to change.
5. If I want to, tell my safe person: "I slipped."

What I have learned
1. You do not need to feel ready: No. Mixed feelings are a normal part of change. Start with one small step, and let your own reasons carry it.
2. Urges are waves: An urge rises, peaks, and passes. You do not have to fight it or obey it. Notice it, breathe, and outlast this one.
5. Name the act, not yourself: Describe what you did, not who you are: “I slipped last night,” not “I am a failure.” Then protect your next good move.
8. Wanting to be loved: No. A habit is something you do, not a verdict on whether you can love. Honesty and closeness are skills you can start practicing now.
11. What to call it, and who can help: No. You can use your own words. What counts is what it does to your life, and help is there whatever you call it.
12. What getting better looks like: Getting better is growth with setbacks, across a whole life: health, home, purpose, and people. A streak is one part, not the whole picture.
13. Name the feeling: Urges often ride in on a feeling. Name it in a word or two, and it loses some of its grip. Then meet that feeling another way.
15. Move your body: Yes. A short burst of movement eases cravings for a while. When an urge starts, move first, then decide.
17. The first link in the chain: Usually hours earlier, with small choices that look harmless. Catch an early link, while the urge is quiet, and the last one never forms.
20. Fewer fights, not more willpower: Not mostly. People with strong self-control fight temptation less, not more. Arrange your day so the fight happens less, and count the fights you skip.
21. Missing a day: No. A single missed day barely dents a new habit, but misses add up. The day after, come back in the smallest way.
22. When values and habits clash: Ask what bothers you most: losing control, a clash with your values, or both. Each points to different help, and both are real.
23. Plan the empty hour: Do not wait to feel like it. Put a real, small activity in your hardest hour, and do it even if you do not feel like it.
24. What therapy is like: Yes, treatment appears to help, and one kind, CBT, has the strongest support. Ask how a therapist works, and switch if it does not fit.
26. SMART Recovery: four points and a toolbox: Yes. SMART Recovery teaches practical tools for motivation, urges, thoughts and feelings, and a balanced life. You can borrow them with or without a meeting.
28. Why groups help: Groups change who you spend time with, and that is one of the main ways they help. Start small: listen at one meeting, or ask one person to check in.
31. Guilt, shame, and God: Write it honestly, then tell God and one safe person. Guilt can point you toward change. Shame says to hide.

journal.book:
MY PLAYBOOK

Why I am doing this
- Being fully present with the people I love
- Clear mornings and steady energy
- Becoming someone I am proud of

My rule
I log slips instead of hiding them. A slip is data, not a reset.

If this, then that
If I am in bed late at night, then Get up and leave the room for 10 minutes. Water, stretch, tidy something. Then back to bed without my phone.
If I am lonely or low, then Text or call one person. A message counts. Or go somewhere with people around.
If I am bored or idle, then 10-minute walk outside, or 10 minutes on a hobby or project.
If I am stressed or anxious, then Move my body (walk, pushups), then write one sentence about what is stressing me.

If I slip
1. Log it in 30 seconds. No hiding.
2. One small action within the hour: water, step outside, or text someone.
3. No big decisions tonight, and no "I blew it" verdicts.
4. Tomorrow: check in as usual. Nothing resets. Ask what the trigger was and what to change.
5. If I want to, tell my safe person: "I slipped."

What I have learned
1. You do not need to feel ready: No. Mixed feelings are a normal part of change. Start with one small step, and let your own reasons carry it.
2. Urges are waves: An urge rises, peaks, and passes. You do not have to fight it or obey it. Notice it, breathe, and outlast this one.
5. Name the act, not yourself: Describe what you did, not who you are: “I slipped last night,” not “I am a failure.” Then protect your next good move.
8. Wanting to be loved: No. A habit is something you do, not a verdict on whether you can love. Honesty and closeness are skills you can start practicing now.
11. What to call it, and who can help: No. You can use your own words. What counts is what it does to your life, and help is there whatever you call it.
12. What getting better looks like: Getting better is growth with setbacks, across a whole life: health, home, purpose, and people. A streak is one part, not the whole picture.
13. Name the feeling: Urges often ride in on a feeling. Name it in a word or two, and it loses some of its grip. Then meet that feeling another way.
15. Move your body: Yes. A short burst of movement eases cravings for a while. When an urge starts, move first, then decide.
17. The first link in the chain: Usually hours earlier, with small choices that look harmless. Catch an early link, while the urge is quiet, and the last one never forms.
20. Fewer fights, not more willpower: Not mostly. People with strong self-control fight temptation less, not more. Arrange your day so the fight happens less, and count the fights you skip.
21. Missing a day: No. A single missed day barely dents a new habit, but misses add up. The day after, come back in the smallest way.
22. When values and habits clash: Ask what bothers you most: losing control, a clash with your values, or both. Each points to different help, and both are real.
23. Plan the empty hour: Do not wait to feel like it. Put a real, small activity in your hardest hour, and do it even if you do not feel like it.
24. What therapy is like: Yes, treatment appears to help, and one kind, CBT, has the strongest support. Ask how a therapist works, and switch if it does not fit.
26. SMART Recovery: four points and a toolbox: Yes. SMART Recovery teaches practical tools for motivation, urges, thoughts and feelings, and a balanced life. You can borrow them with or without a meeting.
28. Why groups help: Groups change who you spend time with, and that is one of the main ways they help. Start small: listen at one meeting, or ask one person to check in.
31. Guilt, shame, and God: Write it honestly, then tell God and one safe person. Guilt can point you toward change. Shame says to hide.
